I didn't read the article, but I honestly think this is a fantastic idea... if implemented correctly.

The correct implementation would utilize QoS and VLANs to segregate the home owners bandwidth and network from the public wifi access. That would be the correct answer. It would need to broadcast 2 SSIDs, one that the home owner has control over, and one that is preconfigured by the ISP on its own VLAN.

edit:

I read the article and the complaint seems to be $23 extra electricity cost on the consumer for broadcasting another SSID -- even if nobody connects to it.

Does an SSID really draw that much power? That seems far fetched to me.

An hypothetical example of why I disabled it on my router (btw Comcast does it this way):

  1. "Home" SSID on Channel 1.
  2. "Comcast Intruder" SSID was also on Channel 1.

When a guest's bits are traveling on that freq, mine are waiting for its turn. I'm paying for that link and I want mine to run as fast as possible. Physics does not currently (or ever) allow both of our traffic to literally simultaneously travel on the same channel.

It's fine that my ipad, phone, computer, and other devices are sharing that channel because it is my stuff. I understand pulling 7MB/s down from one device will affect the ability for me to maintain a 1080p stream on another. I can decide accordingly how I want to handle data if I need something better or quicker.

I'm not letting some asshole watch Netflix using my channel. It doesn't matter if it is on a different SSID, they still have to use the same radio channel and I won't allow that.

So, let's pretend that Comcast decides to put their guest network on a different channel. Now they're being assholes a different way by taking up more radio channels that I have to share with my neighbors. It's not happening as long as I have control of my connection.

When a guest's bits are traveling on that freq, mine are waiting for its turn. I'm paying for that link and I want mine to run as fast as possible. Physics does not currently (or ever) allow both of our traffic to literally simultaneously travel on the same channel.

This is precisely why it's wrong. Respect the customers' domain. I'm sure people would be glad to host the hotspots for a fee.

Also: fuck the cable wifi coalition. They shove this shit into businesses as "free wifi" when it's only available to the customers of the few cable companies working together. That's not free; it requires subscription!

I read the article and the complaint seems to be $23 extra electricity cost on the consumer for broadcasting another SSID -- even if nobody connects to it.

That number is bullshit, or that is one ridiculously inefficient router. I plugged my router (Archer C9) into my Kill-A-Watt to test, and it pulls between 9W idle and 10.3W full load (torrenting full speed to test), and that's with 2 SSID's (1@2.4GHz and 1@5GHz) and 5 clients. At my current kWh rate, that's between $9.50 and $10.50 per year. Total. There's no way adding another SSID would cost an additional $23/year unless the router is stupid inefficient, or the cost of electricity was stupid high, or both.
